description: Lightning is not magic: it is an enormous electrical discharge inside a storm cloud. Here is how it builds up, and then how it strikes.

hero.hook: In a fraction of a second, the air hits 30,000°C. Five times hotter than the surface of the Sun.

blocks.text: A bolt of lightning releases colossal energy in the blink of an eye. The air inside the lightning channel climbs to roughly **30,000°C**. Thunder is nothing more than the sound of that brutal heat.
To understand lightning, follow three steps: how the cloud builds up its charge, how the electricity finds a path, and why the thunder reaches you afterward.
Lightning is mostly born inside [[cumulonimbus]] clouds: huge storm towers that can rise to about **15 km**. Inside them, air rushes up and down very hard.

In that chaos, small **ice crystals** ride upward while heavier grains of ice ([[sleet]]) fall. Each collision swaps a little electric charge. Bit by bit, the top of the cloud turns positive and the base turns negative.
Lake Maracaibo, in Venezuela, is one of the most lightning-struck places on the planet: storms there are almost a daily event for much of the year.

sections.title: Inside the cloud, charges pull apart

blocks.text: Air is a poor conductor. But if the difference in charge grows too large (often **hundreds of millions of volts**), the air finally gives in. Molecules lose electrons and start to conduct. That is [[ionization of the air]].

An invisible channel leaves the cloud in short jumps. From the ground, electrical streamers reach up, mostly from sharp points: trees, lightning rods, buildings. When the two meet, the circuit closes.

The bright flash we actually see, the **return stroke**, travels mostly from the ground back up to the cloud. The current can reach tens of thousands of amperes. Several discharges can follow one another down the same channel, which is what makes lightning flicker.

sections.title: When the air gives way: the discharge

blocks.text: The bolt heats the air so fast that it expands all at once. That shock wave becomes **thunder**. The light reaches you almost instantly. The sound only travels at about **340 m/s**.
A simple trick: count the seconds between the flash and the thunder, then divide by **3**. That gives you a rough distance in kilometers.
The Earth is hit by about **100 bolts of lightning per second** on average. France alone records around **a million** ground strikes a year.

Lightning remains dangerous, above all out in the open, near lone trees or water. It also starts fires. But it has a less famous effect: it helps make nitrogen compounds that the rain then carries down to fertilize the soil.
Above thunderstorms, cameras have also caught strange phenomena such as [[Sprites]]: brief glows high in the atmosphere, invisible to the naked eye from the ground.

Inside a cumulonimbus, collisions between ice and sleet pull the charges apart. When the voltage grows too strong, the air ionizes: the bolt heats it to about 30,000°C, and that violent expansion makes the thunder.
